title: Three-Quarter Angle
description: A three-quarter angle turns the face about 45 degrees to the camera so both eyes remain visible and the far cheek recedes. It is the standard narrative portrait angle: dimensionality without a full front or a true side.

sections.title: Narrative function

blocks.text: Most coverage of a talking face lives here. You see both eyes, the bridge of the nose, and a cheek going away, which is enough skull to light and enough access to read a listen.

It is useful because it models the head and still connects to an offscreen partner along a natural eyeline. It is the wrong tool when you want a coin (use Profile) or a confession into the taking lens (use Fourth Wall).
It is also not a height: you can shoot three-quarter from Eye Level, Low Angle, or High Angle. The name is yaw, not tilt.

sections.title: How it works

blocks.text: Place the camera about 30 to 50 degrees off the subject's nose. Keep both irises; hide only a sliver of the far ear if any.
A 50mm to 85mm holds the head without stretching the near eye. Key from the far or near side depending on short or broad lighting; the angle is what gives the planes.
Prompt: three-quarter angle, face turned about 45 degrees, both eyes, classic portrait dimensionality.

sections.title: When to use it

blocks.text: Use it as the default narrative portrait when a face must have volume and still belong to a scene. Concrete beat: a diner single, body open 45 degrees, eyeline to the partner off left, both eyes sharp.
Do not use it when concealment is the point; rotate to Profile.

sections.title: Compared with similar shots

blocks.text: Profile is 90 degrees, one ear, far eye gone. Eye Level is how high the camera sits; three-quarter is how the head is turned.
Over-the-Shoulder Coverage often holds a three-quarter far face with a near shoulder chewing the frame. A full-front look into lens is Fourth Wall or an Interview eyeline, not three-quarter.

sections.title: In film

blocks.text: Heat's diner encounter parks two faces in three-quarter so each man remains a full head while screen direction stays clean. Classical portrait coverage from studio-era close-ups through drawing-room films uses the same 45-degree turn to model a cheek.
Borrow the yaw and the two eyes, not a copied booth.

sections.title: Prompt it

blocks.text: Name the turn in degrees and keep both eyes. Quote: Three-quarter angle on [Subject], face turned about 45 degrees, classic portrait dimensionality.
Add: both eyes visible, far cheek receding, not a true profile, not looking into the lens. Specify height separately (eye-level three-quarter, and so on).

sections.title: What usually goes wrong

blocks.text: The usual wrong cousin is Profile (too much turn) or a passport front (too little). Tell: far eye gone, or both ears equally seen.
Fix: about 45 degrees, both irises, one ear dominant. The other failure is calling a Low Angle a three-quarter.
Pitch is not yaw; say both.

sections.title: Questions

blocks.text: What is a three-quarter angle in film?
A three-quarter angle turns the face about 45 degrees to camera. Both eyes stay visible and the far cheek recedes, which is the default narrative portrait.
Three-quarter angle vs profile
Three-quarter keeps both eyes and a receding cheek. Profile is a 90-degree side view: one ear, nose as a line, far eye hidden.
When should I use a three-quarter angle?
Use it for most talking portraits that still need a connection to an offscreen partner. Use profile to withhold, or a look into lens to admit the audience.
How do I prompt a three-quarter angle for AI image or video?
Write: Three-quarter angle on [Subject], face turned about 45 degrees, both eyes visible, far cheek receding. Name camera height separately. Not profile, not into the lens.
